claims.text: The relevant starting material is a solid, mixed, single-source precursor containing at least five noble-metal species.
Accelerating precursor reduction rapidly immobilizes the constituent metal atoms.
Limited atomic mobility can trap atoms in a relatively random, well-mixed nanoparticle configuration.
Suppressing atomic diffusion opposes interaction-driven phase segregation.
The proposed kinetic lock remains effective in systems containing more than five interacting elements.
The intervention changes the rate of conversion of metal precursors to metals while leaving other synthesis conditions unchanged.
Solid single-source precursors reduced at moderate or low temperature have limited species mobility.
The relevant low-temperature solid-phase reduction is performed under an inert atmosphere.
Rapidly formed nanoparticle nuclei become immobilized early enough to prevent significant diffusion and segregation.
Faster and more synchronized precursor reduction shortens the time available for individual atoms to migrate.
Kinetic arrest favors a single-phase high-entropy alloy over phase-separated or elementally segregated structures.
Faster reduction will produce a narrower nanoparticle size distribution than slower reduction.
Faster reduction will produce more uniform elemental mixing and less phase segregation than slower reduction.
The slower-reduction baseline exhibits elemental segregation, nonuniform morphology, and a broader particle-size distribution.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to low-temperature solid-precursor systems in which free-atom mobility is limited.
The hypothesis may not apply to high-temperature or solution-based syntheses because greater mobility allows thermodynamic factors to dominate phase formation.
The qualitative effect of accelerated reduction on phase homogeneity is supported by simulation and comparative evidence.
The quantitative particle-size changes, kinetic thresholds, and optimal temperature regimes are uncertain and may vary among precursor systems.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents accelerated or synchronized reduction as the key cause of single-phase formation, whereas the cited same-system evidence reports that five-element HEA particles formed even when the elements reduced consecutively and instead emphasizes element count plus limited mobility. This is an evidence-level tension rather than a direct contradiction between hypothesis fields.
